Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Welder
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Vignette:
Koa, a 51-year-old welder, sat across from the clinician, his hands clasped tightly in his lap, the calluses on his palms a testament to years of hard physical work. His life had been steady, predictable, until eight months ago, when a routine drive home from his shop shattered everything. He had been navigating the familiar evening traffic when, without warning, a vehicle swerved into his lane, heading straight for him. The screech of tires, the blare of a horn, and then the deafening, bone-jarring impact had thrown his body violently against the confines of his truck. He remembered the excruciating pain in his left leg and chest as the crumpled metal pinned him, the sickening crunch and tear of the vehicle around him. What stood out most vividly was the overwhelming, acrid smell of cheap alcohol that permeated the air, thick and nauseating, as he lay trapped, certain he was going to die.

In the weeks and months that followed the collision, Koa’s physical wounds slowly began to heal, but the unseen injuries festered. He found himself increasingly on edge, a constant state of vigilance shadowing his every move. The world, once familiar, had become a minefield of triggers. A sudden car horn on the road, or the distant screech of tires, would send a jolt through his body, making him flinch violently. He would tense, his heart hammering, as if bracing for another impact. Even the general rumble of traffic outside his welding shop, a sound he had grown accustomed to over decades, now grated on his nerves, making him jump at unexpected noises from the machinery.

What truly terrified Koa, however, was the way the memory of the crash would return. It wasn't just a fleeting thought; it was a complete, terrifying reliving of the event. When these memories came, he felt his body twist and contort into the exact position it had been in during the collision, the crushing weight on his chest and the agonizing, searing pain in his left leg returning with astonishing clarity. The smell of alcohol would fill his nostrils, so potent and real that he would sometimes gag. He would hear the deafening roar of the impact, the shattering glass, the tearing metal, and simultaneously *see* the distorted view of the crumpled dashboard and the approaching vehicle, all as if it were happening again, right then, across all his senses at once. It was so vivid, so visceral, that he often struggled to distinguish it from reality for several terrifying moments.

These intrusive experiences started to dictate Koa’s life. He began to avoid busy roads, taking significantly longer, circuitous routes to his welding shop, hoping to minimize his exposure to other cars. Eventually, the dread of driving became so intense that he started asking his wife, Leilani, to drop him off and pick him up, a change that chipped away at his sense of independence and added a new strain to their daily routine. At work, the need for precision welding became a challenge; the constant fear of a memory striking, combined with his heightened startle response to the shop's loud noises, made him less efficient and more prone to errors, causing him to take more breaks and isolate himself from his colleagues. He had also stopped joining Leilani for their regular Friday night dinners out, the fear of encountering the smell of alcohol in a restaurant or the sight of a minor fender bender on the evening news proving too overwhelming. He came to believe that the crash had irrevocably broken something within him, that he was permanently damaged, and that he would never feel safe or truly present in his own life again. The relentless cycle of vigilance and terrifying reliving, and the growing isolation it caused, was what finally prompted Koa to seek help, desperately hoping to find a way to escape the constant echoes of that horrific night.
